name: Bernhard Riemann
bio: Mathematician whose geometry of curved spaces provided the mathematics of general relativity, and whose hypothesis about prime numbers remains the most famous unsolved problem in mathematics.
bio_full: Riemann was the son of a Lutheran pastor in a village near the Elbe and was shy and often unwell. He studied at Göttingen and Berlin and took his doctorate under Gauss in 1851. He taught at Göttingen, succeeding Dirichlet as professor in 1859. Tuberculosis forced him to seek the Italian climate, and he died on Lake Maggiore at thirty-nine.

In a few highly original papers Riemann transformed complex analysis, introduced the Riemann integral and Riemann surfaces, and in his 1854 lecture on the foundations of geometry described spaces of any number of dimensions whose curvature can vary from point to point. Einstein used this geometry for general relativity. His single paper on prime numbers of 1859 linked their distribution to the zeros of a function, the zeta function, and his conjecture about those zeros, the Riemann hypothesis, is still unproved.

name: Georg Cantor
bio: Mathematician who created set theory and showed that there are different sizes of infinity, some infinite sets being strictly larger than others.
bio_full: Cantor was born in Saint Petersburg to a merchant family that moved to Germany when he was eleven. He studied at Zurich, Berlin and Göttingen and spent his whole career at the University of Halle. His ideas met fierce opposition, especially from Leopold Kronecker, and he suffered recurring bouts of depression from 1884 onwards, spending periods in sanatoriums. He died in a Halle sanatorium during the First World War.

Starting from problems about trigonometric series, Cantor developed a theory of sets and their sizes. In 1874 he proved that the real numbers cannot be put in one-to-one correspondence with the whole numbers, and in 1891 gave his famous diagonal argument showing that for any set there is a larger one. He built an arithmetic of transfinite numbers and posed the continuum hypothesis. Hilbert called set theory a paradise from which no one would drive mathematicians, and it became the common language of modern mathematics.

name: David Hilbert
bio: Leading mathematician of the early twentieth century, who set the agenda of modern mathematics with his 23 problems and sought to place it on secure formal foundations.
bio_full: Hilbert was born and educated in Königsberg, where he formed a lifelong friendship with Hermann Minkowski. In 1895 he moved to Göttingen, which under him and Felix Klein became the world centre of mathematics, attracting students and visitors from everywhere, including Emmy Noether, whom he fought to have appointed. After the Nazis expelled many of his colleagues in 1933, the institute was a shadow of itself, and he died in Göttingen during the Second World War.

Hilbert did fundamental work in invariant theory, number theory, the axioms of geometry, integral equations and the mathematics of physics, where the Hilbert space is named after him. At the 1900 International Congress in Paris he presented a list of problems that shaped twentieth-century research. His programme to prove mathematics consistent and complete by finite formal methods was shown by Gödel in 1931 to be unachievable as he had hoped, but it gave birth to modern logic and proof theory.

name: Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen
bio: Physicist who discovered X-rays in 1895 and was awarded the first Nobel Prize in Physics.
bio_full: Röntgen was the only child of a cloth merchant and grew up in the Netherlands. Expelled from school for a prank he did not commit, he studied mechanical engineering at the Zurich Polytechnic and then physics. He held posts at Strasbourg, Hohenheim and Giessen, and in 1888 became professor of physics at Würzburg, later moving to Munich. He received the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901 and gave the prize money to his university.

In November 1895, experimenting with cathode-ray tubes, Röntgen noticed that a fluorescent screen across the room glowed even when the tube was covered. He spent weeks investigating the invisible, penetrating radiation, which he called X-rays, and made an image of the bones in his wife's hand. Within months X-rays were being used by doctors around the world. Röntgen refused to patent the discovery, believing it belonged to humanity. The discovery also launched the research that led to radioactivity and atomic physics.

name: Marie Curie
bio: Physicist and chemist who pioneered the study of radioactivity, discovered polonium and radium, and was the first person to win two Nobel Prizes.
bio_full: Maria Skłodowska was the daughter of teachers in Russian-ruled Warsaw, where women could not attend university. She worked as a governess to pay for her sister's medical studies, then in 1891 went to Paris to study physics and mathematics at the Sorbonne. In 1895 she married the physicist Pierre Curie. After Pierre's death in a street accident in 1906 she took over his chair, becoming the first woman professor at the Sorbonne. During the First World War she organised mobile X-ray units for the front. She died of aplastic anaemia, almost certainly caused by her long exposure to radiation.

Following Henri Becquerel's discovery of uranium rays, Curie found that the intensity of the radiation depended only on the amount of uranium, suggesting it came from the atom itself, and she coined the word radioactivity. With Pierre she discovered polonium and radium in 1898, and after years of processing tonnes of pitchblende she isolated radium salts. She shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with Pierre and Becquerel, and won the 1911 Nobel Prize in Chemistry alone. Her daughter Irène Joliot-Curie also won a Nobel Prize.

name: Max Planck
bio: Theoretical physicist whose hypothesis that energy is emitted in discrete quanta, made in 1900, began quantum theory.
bio_full: Planck came from a family of scholars and lawyers and studied at Munich and Berlin, where he heard Helmholtz and Kirchhoff. He was professor of theoretical physics at Berlin from 1889 to 1926 and a dominant figure in German science, presiding over the Kaiser Wilhelm Society. He won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1918. His later life was marked by tragedy: his elder son was killed at Verdun, and his younger son was executed in 1945 for involvement in the plot against Hitler.

Working on the problem of how the radiation emitted by a hot body depends on temperature and wavelength, Planck found in 1900 a formula that matched experiment, and could derive it only by assuming that energy is exchanged in packets proportional to frequency, with a new constant now called Planck's constant. He regarded this at first as a mathematical device; Einstein and Bohr showed it to be fundamental. Planck was also an early champion of Einstein's relativity.

name: Ernest Rutherford
bio: New Zealand-born physicist who explained radioactivity as the transformation of elements, discovered the atomic nucleus and first split an atom by artificial means.
bio_full: Rutherford was the son of a flax-miller and farmer in New Zealand. A scholarship took him from Canterbury College to the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge in 1895, where he worked under J. J. Thomson. He was professor at McGill University in Montreal, then at Manchester, and from 1919 director of the Cavendish Laboratory, where many future Nobel laureates trained under him. He won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1908 and was made Baron Rutherford of Nelson.

At McGill, with Frederick Soddy, Rutherford showed that radioactive atoms spontaneously turn into other elements, and he named alpha and beta radiation. At Manchester, experiments by Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden firing alpha particles at gold foil led him in 1911 to propose that the atom's mass is concentrated in a tiny, positive nucleus. In 1917–19 he transformed nitrogen into oxygen by alpha bombardment, the first artificial nuclear reaction, and he identified the proton.

name: Albert Einstein
bio: Theoretical physicist who created the special and general theories of relativity and helped found quantum theory. He became the most famous scientist of the twentieth century.
bio_full: Einstein grew up in Munich, left school without graduating and studied physics at the Zurich Polytechnic. Unable to find an academic post, he worked at the Swiss patent office in Bern, where in 1905 he published four papers that changed physics. He held professorships in Zurich and Prague and from 1914 in Berlin. The 1919 eclipse expedition confirming general relativity made him world-famous, and he won the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for the photoelectric effect. Jewish and a pacifist, he left Germany in 1933 and settled at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton.

Special relativity showed that space and time depend on the observer's motion and that mass and energy are equivalent. General relativity, completed in 1915, explained gravity as the curvature of spacetime by matter and energy and predicted the bending of light, gravitational waves and black holes. His 1905 explanation of the photoelectric effect treated light as quanta, and he made many other contributions to quantum and statistical physics, though he never accepted that quantum mechanics was a complete description of reality. He spent his last decades seeking a unified field theory and speaking for peace and civil rights.

name: Niels Bohr
bio: Physicist who applied quantum ideas to the structure of the atom and led the development and interpretation of quantum mechanics from his institute in Copenhagen.
bio_full: Bohr was the son of a physiology professor in Copenhagen and studied at the university there. In 1911–12 he worked in England, first with J. J. Thomson in Cambridge and then with Rutherford in Manchester. In 1921 he founded the Institute for Theoretical Physics in Copenhagen, which became the meeting place of the new quantum physics. He won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1922. In 1943 he escaped occupied Denmark and took part in the atomic bomb project, afterwards campaigning for openness and international control of nuclear weapons.

In 1913 Bohr proposed that electrons in atoms occupy only certain allowed orbits and emit or absorb light when they jump between them, explaining the spectrum of hydrogen. This model, though soon superseded, linked quantum theory to atomic structure. He then guided the younger physicists who created quantum mechanics and developed the principle of complementarity, at the heart of the Copenhagen interpretation, debating its meaning with Einstein for decades. He also explained nuclear fission with the liquid-drop model.

name: Emmy Noether
bio: Mathematician who discovered the deep link between symmetries and conservation laws in physics and was a founder of modern abstract algebra.
bio_full: Noether was the daughter of the mathematician Max Noether in Erlangen, where women were allowed to enrol at the university only from 1904. She took her doctorate there in 1907 and worked for years without pay. In 1915 Hilbert and Klein invited her to Göttingen, but faculty opposition to a woman lecturer meant she could only teach under Hilbert's name until 1919, and she was never given a full professorship. Dismissed in 1933 because she was Jewish, she moved to Bryn Mawr College in the United States, where she died after surgery two years later.

Noether's theorem of 1918 shows that every continuous symmetry of a physical system corresponds to a conserved quantity: symmetry in time gives conservation of energy, symmetry in space conservation of momentum. It became a guiding principle of twentieth-century physics. In the 1920s her work on rings, ideals and modules transformed algebra into the abstract, structural subject it is today, and she inspired a large circle of students, the 'Noether boys'.

name: Werner Heisenberg
bio: Physicist who created matrix mechanics, the first complete form of quantum mechanics, and formulated the uncertainty principle.
bio_full: Heisenberg was the son of a professor of Greek in Munich. He studied with Arnold Sommerfeld, took his doctorate at twenty-two, and worked with Max Born in Göttingen and with Bohr in Copenhagen. In 1927 he became professor at Leipzig, and he received the Nobel Prize in Physics for 1932. He stayed in Germany under the Nazis and led the German nuclear research programme during the Second World War; how far he worked for or against a bomb remains intensely debated. After the war he directed the Max Planck Institute for Physics.

On the island of Heligoland in 1925 Heisenberg found a way to describe atomic systems purely in terms of observable quantities, which Born and Pascual Jordan recognised as matrix algebra. In 1927 he showed that certain pairs of quantities, such as position and momentum, cannot both be known precisely at once, the uncertainty principle. These ideas, with Bohr's, formed the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics. He later worked on nuclear physics and the theory of elementary particles.

name: Erwin Schrödinger
bio: Physicist whose wave equation became the central equation of quantum mechanics. His book What Is Life? inspired a generation of molecular biologists.
bio_full: Schrödinger studied at the University of Vienna and served as an artillery officer in the First World War. He was professor in Zurich from 1921, where he made his great discovery, and succeeded Planck in Berlin in 1927. Opposed to the Nazis, he left Germany in 1933, the year he shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Paul Dirac, and after periods in Oxford and Graz settled at the Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies from 1939 to 1956, before returning to Vienna.

In 1926 Schrödinger described electrons as waves governed by an equation that gave the energy levels of the hydrogen atom, and showed that his wave mechanics was equivalent to Heisenberg's matrix mechanics. He was unhappy with the probabilistic interpretation, and in 1935 devised the thought experiment of a cat both alive and dead to show its strangeness. His 1944 book What Is Life? suggested that genes contain a coded message in an 'aperiodic crystal', an idea that Watson and Crick both acknowledged as an inspiration.

name: Edwin Hubble
bio: Astronomer who showed that the spiral nebulae are galaxies far beyond the Milky Way and that more distant galaxies recede faster, the observational basis of the expanding universe.
bio_full: Hubble grew up in Missouri and Illinois, studied mathematics and astronomy at the University of Chicago and law at Oxford as a Rhodes Scholar, and briefly taught high school. After a doctorate at Chicago and service in the First World War, he joined the Mount Wilson Observatory in California in 1919, where he had use of the 100-inch Hooker telescope, then the largest in the world. He worked there for the rest of his life, apart from war service in ballistics during the Second World War.

In 1923–24 Hubble identified Cepheid variable stars in the Andromeda nebula and used them to show that it lies far outside our galaxy, settling the debate over whether the universe contains other galaxies. He devised the classification of galaxies by shape still used today. In 1929, combining his distances with redshifts measured largely by Vesto Slipher and with Milton Humason's work, he showed that galaxies recede at speeds proportional to their distance. Lemaître had found the relation two years earlier, and since 2018 it has been officially called the Hubble–Lemaître law. The Hubble Space Telescope is named after him.

name: Georges Lemaître
bio: Belgian priest and physicist who proposed that the universe is expanding and that it began from a 'primeval atom', the idea now called the Big Bang.
bio_full: Lemaître studied engineering at Leuven, fought in the Belgian army in the First World War, then turned to mathematics and physics and was ordained a Catholic priest in 1923. He studied with Arthur Eddington in Cambridge and at Harvard and MIT, and from 1925 taught at the Catholic University of Leuven for the rest of his career. He later became president of the Pontifical Academy of Sciences, and was an early user of electronic computers.

In 1927 Lemaître published, in a little-read Belgian journal, a solution of Einstein's equations describing an expanding universe, with an estimate of the expansion rate from galaxy data, two years before Hubble. In 1931 he proposed that the universe began from a single 'primeval atom', whose decay produced everything since. The idea was later developed by George Gamow and others, and the discovery of the cosmic microwave background in 1965, shortly before Lemaître's death, gave it strong support. He kept his science and faith distinct.

name: Alexander Fleming
bio: Bacteriologist who discovered penicillin in 1928, the first antibiotic, and the antibacterial enzyme lysozyme.
bio_full: Fleming grew up on a farm in Ayrshire, moved to London and worked in a shipping office before a legacy allowed him to study medicine at St Mary's Hospital Medical School. He spent his career at St Mary's, in the inoculation department of Sir Almroth Wright, and served in battlefield hospitals in France in the First World War, where he saw many soldiers die of infected wounds. He shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1945 with Howard Florey and Ernst Chain and was knighted in 1944.

In 1928 Fleming noticed that a mould contaminating a culture plate of staphylococci had killed the bacteria around it. He identified it as Penicillium and named its active substance penicillin, but could not purify it in useful quantities. A decade later Florey, Chain, Norman Heatley and colleagues in Oxford developed it into a drug, and it was mass-produced during the Second World War. Penicillin opened the age of antibiotics, and Fleming warned early that misuse would breed resistant bacteria.

name: Kurt Gödel
bio: Logician who proved that any consistent formal system rich enough for arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove, transforming the foundations of mathematics.
bio_full: Gödel was born into a German-speaking family in Brno and studied mathematics and physics at the University of Vienna, where he took part in meetings of the Vienna Circle of philosophers. He proved the completeness of first-order logic in his doctoral thesis and his incompleteness theorems in 1931. After the annexation of Austria he emigrated in 1940 to the United States, crossing Siberia and the Pacific, and joined the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, where he became a close friend of Einstein. He suffered from paranoia and died of malnutrition, having refused to eat for fear of poisoning.

Gödel's first incompleteness theorem showed that in any consistent formal system that includes arithmetic there are statements that can neither be proved nor disproved within it; the second showed that such a system cannot prove its own consistency. This ended the hope of Hilbert's programme in its original form. He also showed that the continuum hypothesis cannot be disproved from the usual axioms of set theory, and found solutions to Einstein's equations that allow travel into the past.

name: Alan Turing
bio: Mathematician who defined the theoretical idea of the universal computer, led the breaking of German naval codes in the Second World War, and posed the question of machine intelligence.
bio_full: Turing studied mathematics at King's College, Cambridge, and wrote his paper on computable numbers in 1936, then took a doctorate at Princeton under Alonzo Church. During the Second World War he worked at Bletchley Park, designing the electromechanical Bombe used to break Enigma messages and leading the attack on German naval codes. After the war he designed the ACE computer at the National Physical Laboratory and worked on early computers at Manchester. In 1952 he was convicted of homosexual acts and subjected to chemical castration; he died of cyanide poisoning in 1954, ruled a suicide. He received a posthumous royal pardon in 2013.

Turing's 1936 paper described a simple abstract machine that can perform any computation that can be precisely specified, and a universal machine that can imitate any other, the theoretical basis of the stored-program computer; he used it to show that some mathematical problems cannot be solved by any mechanical procedure. In 1950 he proposed the imitation game, now called the Turing test, as a way of asking whether machines can think, and in his last years he did pioneering work on the mathematics of biological pattern formation.

name: Claude Shannon
bio: Mathematician and engineer who founded information theory and showed that Boolean logic could be used to design switching circuits.
bio_full: Shannon grew up in Gaylord, Michigan, studied electrical engineering and mathematics at the University of Michigan and went to MIT, where he worked on Vannevar Bush's differential analyser. His 1937 master's thesis showed that relay circuits could be analysed and designed with Boole's algebra. He worked at Bell Telephone Laboratories from 1941, including wartime work on cryptography, and from 1956 taught at MIT. He was also known for his juggling, unicycling and playful machines.

Shannon's 1948 paper 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication' defined information as a measurable quantity, measured in bits, and showed that every communication channel has a capacity below which messages can be sent with as few errors as desired using suitable codes. It laid the foundation for digital communication, data compression and error-correcting codes. He also wrote early papers on programming a computer to play chess.

name: Rosalind Franklin
bio: Chemist and X-ray crystallographer whose diffraction images and measurements of DNA were essential to the discovery of the double helix. She also did pioneering work on coal and viruses.
bio_full: Franklin came from a prominent London Jewish family and studied chemistry at Newnham College, Cambridge. During the Second World War she studied the structure of coal for the British Coal Utilisation Research Association, and from 1947 to 1950 worked in Paris, where she mastered X-ray diffraction. In 1951 she joined King's College London to study DNA, in a difficult working relationship with Maurice Wilkins. In 1953 she moved to Birkbeck College, where she led important studies of the structure of viruses. She died of ovarian cancer at thirty-seven.

At King's, Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling distinguished two forms of DNA and produced sharp diffraction images, including Photo 51, together with precise measurements showing that the phosphate backbone lies on the outside. Without her knowledge, Wilkins showed Photo 51 to James Watson, and a report containing her data reached Francis Crick; these were crucial to their model. Her contribution was long underplayed, partly because she died before the 1962 Nobel Prize was awarded, and she has since become a symbol of overlooked women in science.

name: James Watson
bio: Biologist who with Francis Crick proposed the double-helix structure of DNA in 1953, and later led the Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory and the early Human Genome Project.
bio_full: Watson entered the University of Chicago at fifteen, took his doctorate at Indiana University on viruses that infect bacteria, and went to Europe as a postdoctoral fellow. In 1951 he joined the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, where he met Francis Crick. He later taught at Harvard, was director and later president of the Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory in New York, and was the first head of the National Institutes of Health genome effort. His late career was overshadowed by repeated public remarks about race and intelligence that led institutions to strip him of honours.

With Crick he built a model of DNA as two helical chains held together by paired bases, using the X-ray data of Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins, and published it in Nature in 1953. Watson, Crick and Wilkins shared the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. His candid memoir The Double Helix (1968) became a bestseller and was criticised for its portrayal of Franklin. His textbooks shaped the teaching of molecular biology.

name: Francis Crick
bio: Physicist turned biologist who co-discovered the structure of DNA with James Watson and did more than anyone to work out how the genetic code is read.
bio_full: Crick studied physics at University College London, and his doctoral research was interrupted by the Second World War, when he designed magnetic and acoustic mines for the Admiralty. Inspired partly by Schrödinger's What Is Life?, he moved into biology and in 1949 joined the Medical Research Council unit at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, where he met Watson in 1951. He spent most of his career in Cambridge and from 1976 at the Salk Institute in California, where he turned to the study of consciousness.

After the double helix of 1953, Crick set out the 'sequence hypothesis' and the 'central dogma' that information flows from nucleic acid to protein and not back, proposed the existence of adaptor molecules, later found to be transfer RNA, and with Sydney Brenner showed in 1961 that the genetic code is read in groups of three bases. He shared the 1962 Nobel Prize with Watson and Wilkins. He was the leading theorist of molecular biology in its classic period.
